bio.en: Sri Batchu is the Head of Growth at Ramp, the fastest-growing SaaS and FinTech company in history (which reached $100M in annualized revenue within two years), and previously served as Head of Growth at Instacart and VP of Operations at Opendoor.
bio.zh: Sri Batchu 是 Ramp 的增长负责人。Ramp 是史上增长最快的 SaaS 与金融科技公司——仅用两年就达到了 1 亿美元年化收入。在此之前，他曾任 Instacart 的增长负责人、Opendoor 的运营副总裁。

summary.en: Ramp seeded its explosive growth with a 'cap table as a growth strategy' — recruiting influential founders and operators as early investors who became its first customers. Its real edge comes from technologizing every channel: a dedicated growth-engineering team automates sales and a shared 'translation layer' maps every team's metric back to a single north-star metric (dollars of SQL pipeline). Culturally, Ramp runs on velocity — working in days not quarters, two-week sprints, calendar audits, and autonomy over hours rather than hours worked. For B2B growth sequencing Sri recommends founder-led sales, then first sales hires, then low-cost targeted marketing (content, community, events, PR), and only later paid, brand, and SEO. He also argues companies should optimize for payback period over CAC or LTV, and design experiments to 'fail conclusively' by maximizing the treatment effect rather than iterating timidly.
summary.zh: Ramp 之所以能爆发式增长，起点是它把「股权结构表当成增长策略」——拉拢有影响力的创始人和运营者成为早期投资人，而这些人又成了它的第一批客户。它真正的壁垒在于把每个渠道都技术化：一支专门的「增长工程」团队自动化销售流程，并用一套共享的「翻译层」把每个团队的指标都映射回同一个北极星指标（销售合格线索带来的美元金额）。在文化上，Ramp 靠的是「速度」——以天而不是季度为单位工作、两周一个冲刺、做日历审计，看重的是自主权和产出而非工作时长。关于 B2B 增长的顺序，Sri 建议先做创始人主导的销售，再招第一批销售，接着做低成本的精准营销（内容、社群、活动、PR），最后才做付费、品牌和 SEO。他还主张企业应该优化「回收周期」而不是 CAC 或 LTV，并且要做「彻底失败」的实验——把能用的手段都押上，而不是小心翼翼地小步迭代。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: I do think there's actually a general path that most B2B companies take and should take. My view is you start off with founder-led sales, the early team needs to know how to actually sell. Then you hire your first couple of salespeople, then you start some very low cost targeted marketing efforts. So whether it's content, community, small scale events, and then PR, after all of that is when you start paid and brand effort and then SEO probably start around the same time that you start paid marketing efforts. The reason for the progression the way I've described it is the channels get more expensive as you go farther along and they get more effective as you understand more about your customers.
turns.zh: 我确实觉得，大多数 B2B 公司实际上走的、而且也应该走的是一条相对固定的路径。我的看法是，先靠创始人亲自去卖——早期团队必须真的懂得怎么把东西卖出去。然后你招头几个销售，接着再做一些成本很低、很精准的营销动作，比如内容、社群、小规模活动，再然后是 PR。等这些都做完了，才开始投付费和品牌，SEO 大概和你开始做付费营销差不多同时启动。之所以要按这个顺序来，是因为越往后的渠道成本越高，但当你越了解客户，它们的效果也越好、也越能规模化。

turns.zh: 是的，我猜你肯定知道 Packy，他做过一个很棒的分析，把这个结论分享出来，还把我们和一堆其他公司做了对比。他一年前发布的时候，我们是在当时最快达到一亿美元年化收入规模的公司。之后有没有别家超过我不确定，但至少在金融科技这个品类里，据我所知没有。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So you said the fastest growing to a hundred million. I think it took two years to get to a hundred million and run rate, right?
turns.zh: 好。你说的最快达到一亿。我记得从起步到一亿美元年化收入大概花了两年，对吧？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.zh: 这太疯狂了，因为很少有一大笔钱就停在那儿，等一家公司进来直接拿走、从别人手里抢过来、还提供那么大的价值。所以这是个离谱的数字。顺着这个方向再问一个，还有没有什么其他数字可以分享一下，关于 Ramp 的规模，或者它增长的速度？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu

turns.zh: 我们公开披露过，去年我们在之前已经很大的基数上又增长了 4 倍。Okta 最近也发布了一些关于 SMB 和中端市场增长最快的软件公司的数据，Ramp 尽管榜单上很多公司体量比我们小不少，却遥遥领先地是最快的。公司的人数相对于这个增长量来说还是非常精简的。我们今天大概不到 500 人，就能做到这个规模，营收人均肯定比我们一些竞争对手和同行高得多。而且我们有一个非常有想法、很聪明的财务团队，其实我之前在 Instacart 的财务战略负责人也在这边，他们给我们定下了很有野心的增长目标，我很高兴地说，自我加入这 16 到 18 个月以来，我们一直稳定地超额完成那些目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Which is especially challenging in this environment. So it's extra meaningful. Okay, so here's the big question I want to start off with. I know you weren't there at the beginning of Ramp's journey, but from what you know, what do you think the team did early on to seed this level of growth and success other than just building an awesome product that people really love? And if that's the answer, that's fine, but usually that's part of it. I'm curious just like is there some clever unique tactics that they used to help create that incredible growth from the beginning?

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: I think you're certainly right on the product side. Obviously you've recently written about Ramp's product engine with Geoff and that there's been incredible product market fit because of the product team that deeply understood the customer experience and I think that's certainly helped initial word of mouth. One thing that I did want to point out that Ramp did that was interesting is obviously Eric and Karim, the co-founders of Ramp, were previous founders of another company that they had a successful exit on.
turns.zh: 我觉得你在产品这点上肯定是对的。你最近刚和 Geoff 写过 Ramp 的产品引擎，产品团队深度理解客户体验，所以产品市场契合度非常强，我觉得这肯定帮了最初的口碑传播。我想特别指出 Ramp 做了一件挺有意思的事：两位联合创始人 Eric 和 Karim 之前创办过另一家公司，并且成功退出了。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: So they had a strong reputation as founders and came in with the right set of experience to build Ramp and one of the things that they did is what I call cap table as a growth strategy where they did a great job of getting a large number of early stage founders and other influential operators and advisors onto the cap table at the company. And many of our initial customers were these companies that were on the cap table or the founders were on the cap table for. And Ramp today is actually not majority startups or tech companies anymore. The vast majority of our customers are mid-market and enterprise. That's where our revenue comes from. But there's a lot of love among the tech founder community because of the early days, both the product quality as well as all of these investors that Ramp got.
turns.zh: 所以他们作为创始人有很强的人脉声誉，带着正确的经验来打造 Ramp。他们做的一件事我称之为「把股权结构表当增长策略」——他们很聪明地让大量早期创始人、其他有影响力的操盘者和顾问进入了公司的股权结构表。而我们很多最初的客户，就是这些在股权结构表上的公司，或者创始人本身就在股权结构表上。不过今天的 Ramp 其实已经不再是主要以初创公司或科技公司为主了。我们绝大多数客户是中端市场和企业客户，那才是我们收入的来源。但因为早期那些产品的质量，加上 Ramp 拿到的这些投资人的背书，科技创始人圈子里对它的喜爱度非常高。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I have not heard of this strategy before and I didn't know this was actually a big part of the initial story. So is there examples of folks that they had on their cap table that are examples of folks that helped them grow initially like this?
turns.zh: 哇。我之前没听过这个策略，也不知道这其实是早期故事里很重要的一块。那有没有具体的例子，比如哪些在股权结构表上的人，是帮他们早期做增长的？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: One example that I can think of is Eight Sleep founder, he's been very close to the Ramp team, same with the Pod founder and then a bunch of VC firms that are investors in the company are also customers of the company.
turns.zh: 我能想到的一个例子是 Eight Sleep 的创始人，他跟 Ramp 团队非常亲近；还有 Pod 的创始人也是，另外一批投资这家公司的风投机构本身也是这家公司的客户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you know if the strategy there was VCs who connect them to small companies that would use Ramp or is it directly founders of companies that would immediately use Ramp?
turns.zh: 你知道这个策略是让那些把他们介绍给会用 Ramp 的小公司，还是直接就是那些会立刻用 Ramp 的公司创始人？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah, I'll say it was more founders and executives of customers that can use Ramp. Certainly we have a fantastic group of very sophisticated investors who have made introductions to Ramp as well and that helped. But I will say that is not as big of a channel as one might expect because companies have their own decision making frameworks for selecting a product like Ramp and the investor opinion and recommendation matters, but turns out it doesn't matter maybe as much as another customer who's actually used the product that they know or are actually experiencing the product.
turns.zh: 嗯，我要说更多的是会用 Ramp 的客户公司的创始人和高管。当然我们也有一群非常厉害、很老练的投资人，他们也帮 Ramp 做了引荐，这也有帮助。但我要说，这个渠道没有大家想的那么大，因为公司选 Ramp 这种产品有自己的决策框架，投资人的意见和推荐有用，但事实证明，它的重要性可能不如另一个真正用过这个产品、或者正在体验这个产品的客户说的话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing, awesome tactic. I've not heard of that before. In terms of growth, how much of growth of early Ramp was new customers versus expansion within existing customers? Because what's cool about credit card is people spend more, you make more money because you're taking a piece of that. So roughly how much of the growth insanity over the first couple of years was from expansion within existing customers?
turns.zh: 妙招，我以前没听过。从增长的角度，早期 Ramp 的增长里，新客户和现有客户的扩张各占多少？因为信用卡有意思的地方在于，人们花得越多，你赚得越多，因为你从中抽成。所以头两年那种疯狂增长里，大概有多少是来自现有客户的扩张？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Obviously many of our early customers have grown quite a bit and our whole strategy is to save companies time and money so they can redeploy that in other ways for their own growth or other objectives. And we obviously are growing our product suite as well like BillPay, Flex, et cetera, where our customers can spend more money on Ramp and get more value out of Ramp. Having said all of that, what's interesting is that the vast majority of our growth back then and even to this day is via new customer acquisition. It's just we are adding so many more customers that the growth of our customers while strong and important part of our growth lever is not nearly as material as you might think.

turns.zh: 好，说得好。这正好引出我下一个问题：如果你画一个饼图，看 Ramp 是怎么增长的，最好能区分早期和现在，这个饼图长什么样？有哪些切片，Ramp 的增长大概都是从哪些渠道来的，各自占比多少？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Rather than going into the specifics, one thing I'll say about the growth system today is if you were to look at what percentage of our business comes from outbound sales, paid marketing, field, and then a bunch of other channels and then you compare it against industry benchmarks, I think the secret sauce of Ramp is not that we've found a channel that's unique and that we've over-invested or under-invested. I don't think our distribution would be not that far off from looking at other companies at our size and stage.
turns.zh: 与其讲具体数字，我想先说一点关于今天增长体系的事：如果你去看我们业务里有多大比例来自外呼销售、付费营销、实地活动，还有其他一堆渠道，再拿去和行业基准对比，我觉得 Ramp 的秘诀不在于我们找到了一个独特的渠道、然后过度或不足地投了它。我认为我们的渠道分布，跟其他和我们规模、阶段差不多的公司比，并不会差太远。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: I think what we've done differently is we've really focused on making all of those investments very much driven by technology and data. And so one example that I'll give you is that our sales teams are actually incredibly efficient by any metric that we look at and we obviously benchmark them. And the reason for that is because we actually have a growth engineering team that's dedicated to supporting that efficiency but including adjusting third party data and using AI to automate much of their workflow, et cetera. And we've been doing this well before AI has become the buzzword for a lot of folks, but this is something we've had this team for almost two years now that that's been working on sales automation and data to just make our sales teams more efficient. That's just one example, but we've got similar types of mandates for every channel that we invest in and thinking about how do we inform this better customer and prospect data and how do we automate and technologize it so that we can build that competitive mode for each channel.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们真正不一样的地方，是我们非常强调让所有这些投入都由技术和数据来驱动。我给你举个例子：我们的销售团队，无论用哪个指标看都极其高效，我们当然也会给他们做基准对比。原因是我们真的有一支专门支持这种效率的「增长工程」团队，包括调整第三方数据、用 AI 来自动化他们大部分工作流等等。我们在 AI 变成很多人嘴边的热词之前很久就在做这个了，这支团队组建快两年了，一直在做销售自动化和数据，就是为了让我们的销售团队更高效。这只是一个例子，但我们投的每个渠道都有类似的要求——怎么用更好的客户和潜在客户数据来赋能，怎么把它自动化、技术化，从而在每个渠道上建立起竞争壁垒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'd love to learn more about this growth eng team that works with sales. How is that structured maybe as the first question and then just what are their goals? How do you measure their progress and success?
turns.zh: 我很想多了解这支配合销售的增长工程团队。它的结构大概是怎样的，先问这个，然后他们的目标是什么？你怎么衡量他们的进展和成效？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: A lot of companies do it differently. I think what works really well with Ramp is that we have the same shared goal, which is the pipeline driven and the payback period of the channel. It's unique to Ramp where the engineers feel ownership of the quota. They're not owning product metrics or what have you, they're obviously of course interim and input metrics that are important, but they really do feel accountable for the pipeline driven and the efficiency driven by that team. And I think that naturally allows them bottom up to come with the right projects that they think will have maximal impact on efficiency and top line.
turns.zh: 很多公司做法不一样。我觉得在 Ramp 特别好用的一点是，我们有同一个共享目标，就是这条渠道带来的销售管道和回收周期。这在 Ramp 挺独特的——工程师会对配额有主人翁感。他们不背产品指标之类的，当然中间层和输入性指标也很重要，但他们真的会觉得对这条渠道带来的管道和效率负责。我觉得这自然就让他们从下往上，提出他们认为对效率和营收顶端影响最大的正确项目。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what are the sorts of things they do for a sales team? Is it like they help them prioritize leads or is it they help craft their messaging? Which parts are maybe most important?
turns.zh: 那他们具体为销售团队做些什么？是帮他们排优先级找线索，还是帮他们写话术？哪部分可能最重要？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: All of the above, helping find the right prospects, sending them the right messaging as well as prioritizing responses and drafting potential responses for the team as well.
turns.zh: 以上都是。帮他们找到对的潜在客户、给他们发对的信息，还有帮团队排优先级回复、起草可能的回复。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fascinating. How much impact have you seen that has on sales?
turns.zh: 有意思。你看到这对销售有多大影响？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: It's incredibly helpful to our sales team and it's one of our most efficient channels as I've mentioned. So I think that there is something unique about our ability to bring technology to every channel.
turns.zh: 对我们的销售团队帮助非常大，而且就像我说过，这是我们用起来最高效的渠道之一。所以我觉得，能把技术带到每个渠道上，这是我们某种独特的能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Super interesting. Maybe on that topic, can you just talk about how your growth team is structured at Ramp? What are the kind of sub-teams and how do you think about?
turns.zh: 特别有意思。顺着这个话题，你能讲讲 Ramp 的增长团队是怎么组织的吗？有哪些子团队，你是怎么考虑的？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: We've got an organization today that might evolve and if we get to that topic we can talk about it, but historically the way we've been organized is we've got channel based teams that are deploying spend in a given channel. So we've got a paid marketing team, a lifecycle CRM team, we've got a field marketing team, et cetera. And then we've got a product engineering team that is supporting growth and sales and helping each of these channels be more effective that's dedicated to growth. And then separate from that, we've got a small kind of what I call an innovation or skunk work type of team that works on cross-channel. Just things that don't neatly fit into a box that we think could be cool or fun to try to just do more experimentation that is cross-channel, cross-team.
turns.zh: 我们现在这个组织形态以后可能还会变，如果聊到那个话题我们可以再谈。但历史上我们的组织方式是按渠道分的团队，各自在某个渠道里投放预算。所以我们有付费营销团队、生命周期 CRM 团队、实地营销团队等等。然后我们有一支支持增长和销售的「产品工程」团队，专门帮这些渠道变得更有效。另外，我们还有一个小规模的、我称之为创新或者「臭鼬工厂」式的跨渠道团队，专门做那些不太能归到某个框里、但我们觉得酷、值得一试的跨渠道、跨团队的实验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Definitely sounds like the most fun team. What are some of the things they've done or work on in the skunk works team?
turns.zh: 听起来绝对是最好玩的团队。他们在臭鼬工厂团队里做过或正在做什么？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: They've done testing of new channels that don't necessarily fit into very... And that includes new online platforms. They've done some interesting stuff on TikTok and Reddit and other places, things like that. They've focused on referrals and how to make that a more delightful experience for the customers, first party events, things like that. Things that are often smaller scale and if they work we can invest more and make them larger scale later.
turns.zh: 他们测试过一些不太容易归类的渠道，包括一些新的线上平台。他们在 TikTok、Reddit 这些地方做过一些有意思的东西。他们专注于推荐机制，怎么让客户的推荐体验更愉悦，还有自有活动之类的。这些通常规模比较小，如果行，我们就多加投入、后面做大规模。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. So the teams roughly is there's a paid growth team that just works on paid growth optimization, lifecycle CRM team basically it's like emails I imagine is a big part of that.
turns.zh: 我喜欢。所以团队的划分大概是：有一个付费增长团队专门做付费增长优化；生命周期 CRM 团队，基本上我猜邮件是很大的一部分。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Then there's a field sales support team and then there's the sales team, kind of eng sales team that you talked about and then I also imagine there's like a self-serve.
turns.zh: 然后有一个实地销售支持团队，还有你提到的那支销售工程团队，然后我猜还有一个自助式的团队。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. There's a self-serve activation eng team as well. And then of course there's SEO and website and bound lead channel management team.
turns.zh: 对，没错。还有一个自助激活的工程团队。当然还有 SEO、网站和入站线索渠道管理团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then this awesome skunk works team. I love it. Okay, so shifting a little bit, something that comes across often and consistently with Ramp, and this came across very clearly in the post that I did on how Ramp builds product with Geoff is velocity and how important velocity is at Ramp. There's this awesome quote that I'll read here from Keith Rabois who I think led many of the rounds of Ramp. He started Founders Fund, famous investor. He said that, "Ramp's product velocity is absolutely unprecedented in my 21 years working with technology businesses." So here's my question to you. Can you just talk about what that actually looks like and feels like working inside Ramp with this intense velocity?
turns.zh: 再加上这个超棒的臭鼬工厂团队。我喜欢。好，稍微转个弯，Ramp 给人感受最强烈、也最一致的一点，就是我在那篇写 Ramp 怎么和 Geoff 做产品的文章里也非常清楚地看到的——「速度」，以及它的重要性。这里有一句很棒的引述，我读一下 Keith Rabois 的话，我觉得他主导了 Ramp 的好几轮融资。他是 Founders Fund 的创始人，著名投资人。他说：「在我从事科技行业 21 年里，Ramp 的产品速度绝对是前所未有的。」所以我要问你的是：在 Ramp 内部，这种强烈的速度感到底是什么样、什么感觉？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah, it is a great question and Keith is amazing and then probably one of the smartest investors that I've ever had a good fortune of working with both here as well as at Opendoor, and I'll say he's absolutely right about that. And what you see internally is what I'll say is razor-sharp focus on reducing cycle time and bias to action and how do we reduce cycle time. I think it's basically the core of it culturally to me is getting people to think about smaller units of time for decision making. It seems obvious but I think you really have to reinforce it culturally. So one thing that Eric, our CEO, does, which I don't know if you've heard externally, is we have days.ramp.com where we can see how many days it's been since the founding of Ramp internally and it's day 1,529 at Ramp. He has that number of days at every board meeting, at every all hands.
turns.zh: 对，这是个好问题，Keith 很厉害，也是我有幸合作过最聪明投资人之一，无论是在这儿还是 Opendoor 都是。我得说他说的完全对。你在内部看到的是，我们极度聚焦于缩短周期时间、行动导向，以及怎么缩短周期时间。我觉得文化上核心就是让人习惯用更小的时间单位来做决策。这听起来很明显，但我觉得你真的得在文化上不断强化它。我们的 CEO Eric 做的一件事——不知道你在外面听没听过——我们有 days.ramp.com 这个网站，能看到 Ramp 成立至今过了多少天，现在是第 1529 天。他在每一次董事会、每一次全员大会上都挂着这个数字。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: It's just to remind people that we don't work in years, quarters, weeks, we work in days. Each day matters and so never put out something tomorrow that you know can get done today. And that bias to action really permeates not just in the product teams but everywhere. So our growth team, which as I've just described, is extremely cross-functional, a lot of marketing folks and other expertise on the team, but we work a lot like a product team, we work on two-week sprints, we cross-prioritize across these teams and we work all together rather than in separate silos within the growth team.
turns.zh: 就是为了提醒大家，我们不是按年、按季度、按周工作，我们是按天工作。每一天都重要，所以凡是今天能做完的，绝不要拖到明天。这种行动导向不只是渗透在产品团队，而是无处不在。比如我们增长团队，就像我刚描述的，跨职能程度极高，团队里有很多营销和其他专业的人，但我们工作起来很像产品团队：我们按两周一个冲刺来跑，跨团队一起排优先级，是作为一个整体在协作，而不是在增长团队内部各自为政、形成孤岛。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I pulled up the site you just mentioned, days.ramp.com, and not only is it days since launch, which is 1,529 when I'm looking at it, there's a many decimal points that are counting up. 1,529.43453142. Oh my god. Okay. Is that a new addition, the decimal points?
turns.zh: 我刚打开你提到的那个网站 days.ramp.com，上面不只有自上线以来的天数，我看的这会儿是 1529 天，后面还有好几位小数在往上跳。1529.43453142。天哪。这个小数点是新加的吧？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: No, I think that's always been there. It's just amping it up, how much time is passing. It could be stressful at times, but I think that the mitigating factor is that it's been able, as you know, A players want to work with A players attract A players and retain A players, and Ramp has done a really great job of hiring people that are fantastic that can work in this environment well and are motivated by the success and the winning from this sort of culture.
turns.zh: 不，我觉得一直都有。就是把这个时间流逝感再加码。有时候确实会有点让人紧张，但我觉得能抵消这个的因素是，正如你所知，A 级人才吸引 A 级人才、留住 A 级人才，而 Ramp 在招到能在这种环境里出色工作、并因这种文化带来的成功而受到激励的牛人这方面，做得非常好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I was actually talking to Eric about it for another piece I'm working on and he was showing me some early board decks in every deck as you said has day 544 of Ramp. So it's very real what you're talking about. Is there anything else that just as someone that came into Ramp from other traditional companies that also move really fast, Instacart and Opendoor, that is just like holy moly, this is velocity? You talked about a few things but is there anything just like holy shit?
turns.zh: 对，其实我为了另一篇在写的文章跟 Eric 聊过，他给我看一些早期董事会的 deck，每一份上面都像你说的写着「Ramp 第 544 天」。所以你说的这个是真的。作为一个从其他也很快的传统公司——Instacart 和 Opendoor——过来的人，有没有什么让你觉得「我的天，这就是速度」的？你说了几点，但还有没有那种让你震惊的？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: You can see the cycle time thing in terms of responsiveness from everybody at Ramp and I think typically what you tend to see is as companies get bigger, they evolve off of Slack to email and everything just moves a little bit slower and there's process and then there's obviously a lot of good parts of that but Ramp, what I noticed when I joined and true to this day is how quickly people will respond on Slack and jump on things and even if they don't complete it, there's very clear action item on who the owner will be and what the deadline will be even if it's not. And that to me was always very impressive just about... And I think it's one of those things we build in public, so everything is very visible so you can see how this is working across teams and I'm glad that we've been able to maintain that culture even as we've gotten much bigger.
turns.zh: 你能从 Ramp 每个人的响应速度上看到这种周期时间的文化。通常你会发现，公司变大之后，会从 Slack 迁移回邮件，一切都慢一点，也开始有流程了——当然这有很多好处。但我加入时注意到、直到今天依然如此的是，大家在 Slack 上回复和响应有多快，马上就扑上去处理，哪怕没做完，也会很清楚谁是负责人、截止日期是什么，哪怕其实没那么紧急。这一点一直让我印象很深——而且我觉得这是我们「公开构建」的一部分，一切都高度可见，你能看到跨团队是怎么运作的。我很高兴即使我们变大了这么多，也还能保持这种文化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's two effects of that I imagine. One is how do you stay in the flow and get work done if you're just expected to constantly respond? How does that actually work?
turns.zh: 我能想到这有两个效应。一个是，如果大家被期待随时响应，那你怎么保持心流、把活干完？这到底是怎么运作的？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: I don't think the expectation is necessarily that one constantly responds, but it is something that I have seen people are good at. And so I think one of the things that, again, not like a novel productivity tool, but something that Ramp does do is just trying to think about focus time and response times and using calendar blocking to really effectively manage your time that way. And then doing calendar audits of yourself as well as of your team to say, okay, what are your highest priorities for this week, this day, this month? And how does your calendar reflect your priorities? Because in many ways you ship your calendar and so thinking about how are you spending your time and then blocking your time accordingly.
turns.zh: 我不觉得大家的预期是必须一直秒回，但我确实看到人们很擅长这件事。所以有一点，再说一次，这不是什么新奇的效率工具，但 Ramp 确实在做的是认真思考专注时间和响应时间，用日历块来有效管理自己的时间。然后还会对自己和团队做日历审计，问：这周、今天、这个月你的最高优先级是什么？你的日历反映出了你的优先级吗？因为在很多层面上，你的日历就是你交付的东西，所以要思考你把时间花在哪了，然后相应地把它锁起来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And is this mostly a cultural just this is how we operate or is there a principles or sorts of processes that are set up to help people do those sorts of things?
turns.zh: 这是主要靠文化——我们就是这么运作的，还是说有一套原则或流程来帮助大家做这些事？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah, it's cultural in terms of how we operate, but we also have templates. Our people team has a template on how to do a calendar audit properly and things like that. So we've tried to create some learning materials as well for folks that are new to get into the flow of way of working.
turns.zh: 对，运作上是文化，但我们也准备了模板。我们的人事团队有一个怎么正确做日历审计的模板之类的。所以我们也试着为新来的人准备一些学习材料，帮他们进入这种工作流的节奏。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, so then the other elephant in the room with talking about working really fast and hard and responding really quickly is work-life balance and burnout and things like that. One thing I'll say is I believe in working really hard and working long hours as a important ingredient to success. I know there's been a bit of a backlash against that and just like, no, you shouldn't work really hard, you can be successful without doing that. I don't think that's true. So with that said, I guess what have you learned and what do you think Ramp has learned about how to find that balance and not just-
turns.zh: 很好。那聊快、拼命干、秒回，房间里另一头的大象就是工作生活平衡、 burnout 这些。我想说一点：我相信拼命干、长时间工作，是成功的重要成分。我知道最近有点反弹，说「不，你不该那么拼命，不那样也能成功」。我不觉得那是真的。说了这些，你学到了什么？你觉得 Ramp 学到了什么，关于怎么找到平衡，而不只是——

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah. I completely agree with you. I do think, especially earlier in your career, hard work is so important both for learning but also impact and it's a tough balance that a lot of successful companies struggle with. I think my biggest learnings is it's, A, some of it is like self-selection, right? You're hiring people that are excited about doing this work and this way of working, but at least I tend to find the people that I've worked with that are highly successful, ours are not the problem. It's really autonomy, flexibility, and mission alignment and the general happiness they get from their work. And so that's what I try to focus on, which is not the hours that someone's put in, but quality of the work and the impact. And I think a big part of the push to having great results and working hard is really being grateful and appreciating the team when they do push themselves and celebrating wins.
turns.zh: 对，我完全同意你。我确实觉得，尤其在你职业生涯早期，拼命干特别重要，既是为了学习，也是为了产出。这是个很多成功公司都挣扎的难平衡。我最大的体会是，首先，一部分是自我选择——你招的是对这种方式、这种工作兴奋的人；但我发现，我合作过的高成功人士，问题从来不在他们身上，而在于自主权、灵活性、使命契合度，以及他们从工作里得到的总体幸福感。所以我专注的就不是某人投入了多少小时，而是工作的质量和影响。而且我觉得，要拿到好结果又拼命干，很重要的一点是当团队拼的时候，你要真心感激、欣赏他们，并且庆祝胜利。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: And I think we could always be doing a better job, but I think we've historically done a great job at that, at celebrating wins big and small. And I think part of the culture of building in public and open internally helps with that. So people are always sharing their wins. And then it's a very one funny stat that I don't know if other companies track is we track engagement during all hands on the Zoom to see what percentage people participate. And it's usually close to a hundred percent, like people are talking, the entire company is talking on the Zoom chat because they're excited about the wins that their friends and colleagues are shipping and the things that we're talking about in the audience.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们永远可以做得更好，但历史上我们在这一点上做得很好——大小胜利都庆祝。而「公开构建」、内部开放的文化也帮了忙，所以大家一直在分享自己的胜利。还有一个很好玩的、我不确定别的公司会不会追踪的数据：我们在全员大会的 Zoom 上追踪参与度，看有多大比例的人在发言。通常接近百分之百——大家在聊天框里说话，整个公司都在 Zoom 聊天里聊，因为他们对朋友和同事交付的东西、对我们在聊的话题感到兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you actually track engagement? Someone sitting there watching who's in the chat?
turns.zh: 你到底怎么追踪参与度？是看谁坐在那儿看、谁在聊天？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: No, it must be some tool our IT team can do it. It can say what percentage of participants chatted or something like that.
turns.zh: 不，肯定是我们 IT 团队用什么工具能做到，能说有多少比例的参与者发了聊天之类。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see. So it's not like who's looking at the screen, it's like who's talking in the chat?
turns.zh: 我明白了。所以不是看谁盯着屏幕，是看谁在聊天里说话？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. Or reacting in the chat, et cetera.
turns.zh: 对，没错。或者在聊天里互动之类的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's awesome. And it's not like you must engage, it's more just like are we delivering the content.
turns.zh: 这很棒。而且不是「你必须参与」，更像是在看「我们交付的内容有没有价值」。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: No. And by the way, this is probably the first time I'm sharing this. I don't think brand employees necessarily know this. I don't think we've actually shared this. I just heard it from our IT person recently and I thought that was a fun stat.
turns.zh: 不是。顺便说，这可能是我第一次分享这个。我觉得品牌部门的员工未必知道。我们其实没公开过。我是最近从 IT 的人那儿听来的，觉得这是个好玩的数据。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that because it's more just like are we providing value to people or are they actually excited and interested in this sort of thing? I was going to add onto your point about how working hard and working long hours can be seen as this like, "Oh, this sucks. I wish I was at home watching Netflix," but I find that the most fulfilling parts of my career or where I was just working insanely hard for a long time, as long as that work was meaningful, exactly like you said, it was something that mattered and came out and shipped and people were excited about it and if it wasn't like, "Oh, that was a waste of my life." So that super resonates.
turns.zh: 我喜欢，因为它更像是在看「我们有没有给大家提供价值，还是他们真的对这类东西感到兴奋和感兴趣？」我本来想接着你那个点说：拼命干、长时间工作会被看成「哦，这太糟了，我宁愿在家看 Netflix」，但我发现我职业生涯里最有成就感的阶段，恰恰就是我为一个长期目标拼命干的时候——只要那工作有意义，就像你说的，它真的重要，最后做出来、发布了，大家很兴奋。如果没意义，那就是「哦，浪费了我的人生」。所以这点我特别有共鸣。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back to growth for a moment. I had a couple more questions I wanted to ask here. You talked about some of these teams that you have around ways you're driving growth. Is there an area you think you're going to be investing more in over time or that you feel is working better? I know there's trade secrets here that you don't want to share necessarily, but just anything that you feel is people are maybe under-appreciating or under-investing in that you think you might invest in more?
turns.zh: 我想回到增长这块一会儿。我还有几个问题想问。你讲到你周围有一些驱动增长的团队。有没有哪个领域，你觉得随着时间你会投更多，或者你觉得现在效果更好的？我知道这里有些商业机密你不一定想分享，但有没有什么是你觉得大家低估了、投少了，而你可能会多投的？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: What I'll say on that front is, look, we, like everybody else, are always focused on driving more efficiency in our growth engine. There are some channels that, and we have a diversified portfolio of bets, right? One thing that's interesting about the world of growth today is I think historically people that used to run growth were folks that had a marketing or a product background. And what you're seeing these days I think are more folks like me who actually come from an investor and analytics background to lead growth teams because growth has become more and more about a diversified portfolio of bets at a reasonable ROI and building a system that's designed around experimentation and data-oriented.
turns.zh: 关于这点我要说的是，跟所有人一样，我们永远在聚焦提升增长引擎的效率。我们有一系列多元化的押注组合，对吧？今天增长世界里一个有趣的现象是，历史上跑增长的人，背景通常是营销或产品。而你现在看到的更多是像我这样、其实是从投资人和分析背景出来的人来领导增长团队，因为增长越来越变成关于一个在合理 ROI 下的多元化押注组合，以及搭建一套围绕实验和数据导向的系统。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: So the reason I say all of that is our goal is to over time, of course, make all of our channels more efficient, but also allocate more to channels that are more efficient as long as they're scalable. And so the more that we can push customer awareness via owned and earned media, the better for us. And so we've got a few different strategies on that front, but we're also working on making our other channels more efficient by the day.
turns.zh: 所以我讲这些的原因是，我们的目标当然是随着时间让所有渠道都更高效，但也会把更多预算分配到更高效、同时又能规模化的渠道上。所以我们越能通过自有和赢得的媒体来推高客户认知，对我们越好。这方面我们有几个不同的策略，但我们也每天在让其他渠道更高效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So mysterious, but I appreciate you sharing what you can. The point about the portfolio of bets is interesting because if you think about it, most companies initially grow from one. You talked about growth engines, that's the same term I use. Usually there's just one thing that helps you grow initially like SEO or word of mouth or maybe paid. And then eventually every single company basically ends up doing all the growth channels and then has a team dedicated to just keep optimizing SEO, keep optimizing referrals. So I think that's a very typical path. And then it's exactly said, how do we make each of these as efficient as possible?
turns.zh: 很神秘，但我感谢你尽量分享。关于「押注组合」这个点很有意思，因为你想想，大多数公司最初都是靠一个渠道起家的。你讲增长引擎，我也用同一个词。通常初期就一件事帮你增长，比如 SEO、口碑，或者付费。然后最终每家公司基本都会把所有增长渠道都做一遍，再专门组个团队一直优化 SEO、一直优化推荐。所以我觉得这是条很典型的路径。然后就像你说的，我们怎么让每一个都尽可能高效？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe as another last question around Ramp's growth. Is there any other just really surprising, interesting, really effective tactics that helped Ramp grow over time?
turns.zh: 那作为关于 Ramp 增长的最后一个问题。有没有其他那种真的让人惊讶、有意思、特别有效的招数，帮 Ramp 一路增长起来的？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: I think one thing that's been interesting is Ramp's ability to leverage PR as a growth machine. And as you've seen, we've got a fantastic PR and comms team and we get a lot of deserved good press through that. And one thing that's been interesting is our fundraising also as a growth strategy not obviously explicitly we've got very clear goals for our fundraising, but what we have seen is anytime that we've been fundraising and we've been using that as an effective way of creating a market moment, it's driven actually a non-trivial amount of top funnel for us.
turns.zh: 我觉得有意思的一点，是 Ramp 把 PR 当成增长机器的能力。你也看到了，我们有一个很棒的 PR 和品牌传播团队，也确实因此拿到了很多应得的、好的媒体报道。还有一点有意思的是，我们的融资本身也是一种增长策略——当然这不是明着说的，我们融资有非常清晰的目标，但我们确实发现，每当我们融资、并把它当成制造一个市场时刻的有效手段时，它其实给我们带来了不小的顶层漏斗。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: People always talk about PR being like, people over overinvest in PR, they think PR is going to be this magical growth lever, but it actually works sometimes and in my opinion, you have to have something really interesting for it to work and obviously you guys do, the company's growing like crazy, which is innately an interesting story. The founders are really important and rarely is funding like an event anymore for most companies. So I mean this says a lot that people care about your funding.
turns.zh: 大家总说 PR 被过度投资了，觉得 PR 会是个神奇的增长杠杆，但有时候它确实有用；在我看来，你得真有特别有意思的东西它才管用，而你们显然有——公司增长疯了一样，这本身就是一个天然有趣的故事。创始人也很重要，而且现在对大多数公司来说，融资已经很少是个「事件」了。所以能让人关心你们的融资，这本身说明了很多。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: What you say it is exactly right is you have to be thoughtful about your PR moments. Everybody wants to announce things about themselves that's not necessarily interesting for the press or for an audience. And so thinking about how do you compile enough value to the general audience. So our fundraising announcements usually also have some additional color on something unique about the business that we share to provide more value to readers.
turns.zh: 你说的完全对，就是你得对你的 PR 时刻很讲究。每个人都想宣布关于自己的事，但对媒体或受众来说那不一定有意思。所以要思考怎么给普通受众凑够价值。所以我们融资的公告通常还会附带分享一些关于业务的独特亮点，给读者提供更多价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then there's also newsletter people like me and Packy you mentioned who wrote about Ramp because it's also just so interesting. What's your sense of that versus traditional PR? There's this, I don't know, big debate of just traditional media's no longer relevant. All these other people will go through newsletters and podcasts and things like that. What's your sense there?
turns.zh: 还有像我和你提到的 Packy 这类写通讯的人，会写 Ramp 因为它也确实太有意思了。你觉得这个和传统 PR 比怎么样？现在有个大辩论，说传统媒体不再 relevant 了，大家都走通讯、播客这些。你怎么看？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: It's what are the audiences that you get with each of these tactics. And so we do both obviously get some earned coverage in these newsletters and other tactics and we pay for some and we advertise in other cases. And what we tend to find is these are great reach, but they tend to work very well for actually hiring. It improves Ramp's reputation as a company for recruiting and hiring, which helps and they help with certain audience of customers, which is typically tech founders and folks close to the tech ecosystem. But as I mentioned, the vast majority of the world is not startups and the majority of Ramp's customers are no longer tech and startups. And so as we're thinking about ways to grow. I think channels like these are one piece of the equation, but I think traditional PR will remain another really important piece because they just target a different audience.
turns.zh: 这要看你通过每种打法能触达到什么受众。我们两种都做，显然在这些通讯和其他打法上拿到一些赢得的报道，有些我们付费，有些我们投广告。我们发现这些触达很广，但对招聘其实特别好用。它提升了 Ramp 作为公司的招聘声誉，这有帮助，也帮到某些客户受众——通常是科技创始人和靠近科技生态的人。但就像我说过，世界上绝大多数不是初创公司，而 Ramp 的大多数客户也不再是科技和初创公司。所以在思考怎么增长时，我觉得这类渠道是等式里的一块，但传统 PR 会一直是另一块很重要的拼图，因为它们针对的是完全不同的受众。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As you're talking, I'm watching the days count up on the days that Ramp page still and stressing me out. I feel like keeping you from doing work to keep growing Ramp, but let's keep going. I'm going to close this tab. You talked about growth engines. I'm curious what you've learned about building a growth engine in a company. And another way to put it is just a repeatable scalable growth process, whether it's at Ramp or Opendoor, Instacart,
turns.zh: 你讲的时候，我看着 days.ramp.com 上的天数还在往上跳，搞得我有点焦虑。我觉得我好像在拖着你、不让你去继续让 Ramp 增长，但我们继续。我把这个标签页关了。你讲了增长引擎。我很好奇你关于在一家公司搭建增长引擎学到了什么。换个说法，就是一个可重复、可规模化的增长流程，无论是在 Ramp、Opendoor 还是 Instacart。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: People talk a lot about what should the right design of the team be or profiles of people on the team, et cetera. And I'm happy to talk about what are the right profiles of people. I think that's an important conversation. But I think design of the team, people often... I think it's a red herring about team structure and team design and what's the right one, et cetera. I think most of that is irrelevant. What actually matters is culture and rituals and cadences rather than the team itself.
turns.zh: 大家聊很多团队该怎么设计、团队里该有什么画像等等。我很乐意聊什么是合适的人画像，我觉得那是个重要话题。但我觉得团队设计、团队结构、什么是对的，这些往往是个红鲱鱼。我觉得那些大多无关紧要。真正重要的是文化、仪式和节奏，而不是团队本身。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: And so what a great growth engine and a great growth team is one that where you set the culture, set very simple north star metrics, usually one, at most two. And you've created a culture of defining hypotheses that are data driven and a culture where that can be executed quickly and have an MVP mentality for product and non-product projects where people can fail and learn quickly and iterate quickly. So I think that part of it is more important than the specific people or their functions in many ways to me, especially when you're starting to build a growth engine. It's like can you build a set of people that can generate new ideas and evaluate them effectively and move quickly is really what you're trying to design for.
turns.zh: 所以一个出色的增长引擎、一支出色的增长团队，是那种你定下文化、定下非常简单的北极星指标（通常一个，最多两个），并且营造出一种文化：用数据驱动来定义假设，有一种能快速执行的 MVP 心态——无论产品还是非产品的项目，人们能快速失败、快速学习、快速迭代。所以我觉得这部分，比具体的人或他们的职能，在很多层面上更重要，尤其是当你刚开始搭增长引擎时。关键是你能不能组建一群能产生新点子、有效评估、并快速行动的人，这才是你要设计的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's unpack some of this because this is great. So in terms of north star metrics, what are some examples in your experience of good north star metrics? Revenue is obviously a very common one, but often it is too high level. Do you have a sense of what a good north star metric is?
turns.zh: 我们把这拆开聊聊，因为这很棒。关于北极星指标，以你的经验，好的北极星指标有哪些例子？营收显然很常见，但往往太高层了。你对什么是好的北极星指标有概念吗？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: I like having two. One is something around volume and growth and you want that to be, A, very motivating and intuitive for people to understand and also, B, something that the growth teams can directly impact, right? Revenue is, for better or worse, more important to the company, but also much farther down the line of whether or not the growth team can impact that. And so at Instacart, for example, our north star metric for growth was monthly active orders. And that's what we all rallied around and looked at every day, how are now doing? And then obviously we had a large growth in consumer engineering team at Instacart, 300 plus people. And so there are people working on every single corner of the app and outside of the app on acquisition to drive growth. And it's like some of the stuff is minutia, right? It's making the checkout flow slightly better or faster or something like that.
turns.zh: 我喜欢用两个。一个是关于量和增长的，你希望它，第一，让大家很有动力、很直觉地理解；第二，是增长团队能直接影响的。营收嘛，不管好坏，对公司更重要，但它离「增长团队能不能影响它」也远得多。所以在 Instacart，我们增长的北极星指标是月活跃订单数。那就是我们所有人每天围着转、每天看「现在怎么样了」的东西。显然 Instacart 当时有个很大的消费者工程团队，300 多人。所以有人在优化 App 里里外外的每一个角落，从获客到驱动增长。有些东西很细枝末节，比如让结账流程稍微好一点、快一点之类的。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: So that's a good example. It's like, okay, well, so we're going to goal that team on MAO, how are they going to move monthly active orders by making the checkout flow slightly better? Maybe they can have an impact or maybe not. And so one of the things that we did is the actual local team has their own metric that they can directly influence. You want to actually hold people accountable for things that they can influence. And then we created via the finance and data team, a translation layer for every team's metric into MAO.
turns.zh: 这是一个好例子。就是我们给那个团队定 MAO（月活跃订单）的目标，他们怎么通过把结账流程改好一点点来拉动月活跃订单？也许有影响，也许没有。所以我们做的一件事是，本地团队有自己的、能直接影响的指标。你要让人对他们能影响的东西负责。然后我们通过财务和数据团队，给每个团队的指标到 MAO 之间建了一层翻译。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: It would be like if you got one extra weekly order because of your checkout flow from the same customer, it would have point X impact on the company's MAO and then you would just roll up all project plans as well as project impact back into this singular MAO metric. And the other benefit of doing something like that is that it also helps you cross-prioritize much easier. Should we add more engineering to this team? Should we add more budget to that team? It's like, okay, well what's the MAO map? Where is there a more MAO per dollar or per engineer being built? And it just really helped us unify and move together.
turns.zh: 就好比，如果你的结账流程让同一个客户每周多下了一单，那对公司 MAO 的影响就是 X 点，然后你把所有项目计划、所有项目影响都汇总回这一个 MAO 指标。这么做还有一个好处，就是它让你跨团队排优先级容易多了。我们该给这个团队多加工程资源吗？该给那个团队加预算吗？就看 MAO 地图：哪里的「每美元 MAO」或「每工程师 MAO」更高？它就真的帮我们把大家统一起来、一起往前走。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have questions about this. This is great. By the way, why is it monthly active orders versus just monthly orders? How can you be an inactive order?
turns.zh: 我对此有些问题。这很棒。顺便问，为什么是月活跃订单，而不是干脆月订单？订单怎么会不活跃？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Sorry, orderer.
turns.zh: 抱歉，是「下单者」（orderer）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, okay.
turns.zh: 哦，好。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: So monthly active users basically is what it is, but we call them orders because users can just log in and not order, right.
turns.zh: 所以本质上就是月活跃用户，但我们叫订单，因为用户可能只是登录而不下单。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it.
turns.zh: 懂了。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: You're actually ordering on the platform.
turns.zh: 你是真的在平台上下了单。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I think there was this backlash against users at Facebook. I think it's monthly active people and so I get it. Okay, understood. Interesting. So you find that instead of sub-teams having a different metric that we just know is good. That's one of the variables in the formula of monthly active orders. You actually have a translation that converts that specific metric moving to the north star metric.
turns.zh: 对，我记得 Facebook 当时对 users 有过反弹。我觉得应该是月活跃的人，所以我懂。好，明白了。有意思。所以你发现，子团队不是各自有一个我们知道「好」的不同指标、作为月活跃订单公式里的一个变量，而是你真的有一个翻译层，把那个具体指标的变动换算成北极星指标。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: The team on their day-to-day for their sprints, whatever are looking at their own metric. But for the purpose of planning and resource allocation and reporting, we would use the translation layers to actually just look at everything on a MAO basis.
turns.zh: 团队在日常冲刺里看的是自己的指标。但出于规划、资源分配和汇报的目的，我们会用翻译层，把所有东西统一到 MAO 基础上来看。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Knowing those sorts of formulas are often not perfect, how much weight do you put into that formula specifically?
turns.zh: 我也知道这类公式往往不完美，你具体给这个公式是多大权重？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah. And I think in general the planning process is not perfect. You can have a financial plan in Excel and the reality can diverge quite a bit. The only thing you can be certain of is that you're not going to accomplish exactly the plan. So we did a couple of things to that. One is setting a culture of we know this isn't perfect, this is like 70/30, 80/20, it's to guide. So we wouldn't use the translation factor to make a marginal decision if something is five or 10% off.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得总体上规划流程不完美。你可以在 Excel 里做一个财务计划，现实却可能差很远。你唯一能确定的是，你肯定完不成那个精确的计划。所以我们做了几件事。一是定下一种文化：我们知道这不完美，大概七三开、八二开，它是指引。所以如果某个东西差了 5% 或 10%，我们不会用翻译系数去做一个边缘决策。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Those are done based on judgment because at the end of the day, regardless of what metric framework you use, marginal decisions are marginal for a reason. They're really hard things to decide. And so the framework helped with just reducing the cognitive overload of decision making to only those that are marginal. So the ones that are obvious that are going to have big impact becomes clear even if the measurement framework isn't perfect. And so that's what we use. And the other thing that we just had as cadence is we would actually update all of the translations every six months for the new planning cycle based on new information that we knew on how moving X impacts MAO.
turns.zh: 那些边缘决策是靠判断做的，因为说到底，不管你用什么指标框架，边缘决策之所以是边缘，就是因为它们真的很难决。所以框架的作用，是把决策的认知负担降到只剩那些边缘的。那些明显会有大影响的，即使测量框架不完美，也会变得清楚。所以我们就是这么用它的。另一件我们做成节奏的事是，我们会根据新信息——关于动 X 怎么影响 MAO 的新认知——每六个月更新一次所有翻译系数，进入新的规划周期。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to make it even more real, what are some examples of those lower level metrics? Is it increased conversion of sign up by X percent?
turns.zh: 让这更真实一点，那些低层指标有些什么例子？是注册转化率提升 X% 吗？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Any number of things. It would be actually load time of the app on open. There's a team that's trying to make that faster or more efficient because we know that that impacts whether or not the person actually ends up ordering if it takes five seconds to load versus two seconds to load. And so the full customer experience were all segregated into different teams that were optimizing just like how long does it take to open, number of searches that a user does on the app. We know the people... And number of items that are put into cart, like amount of time from cart to check out, things like that we literally just map out any user's journey throughout the app and have separate engineering teams that are focused on that.
turns.zh: 任何东西都行。比如 App 打开时的加载时间。有个团队在专门让它更快或更高效，因为我们知道，加载要 5 秒还是 2 秒，会影响这个人最后到底下不下单。所以整个客户体验被拆给不同团队，各自优化，比如打开要多久、用户在 App 里搜几次。我们知道……放进购物车的商品数量、从购物车到结账的时间之类的——我们 basically 就是把用户在 App 里的整个旅程画出来，分给不同的工程团队去专注。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And there's essentially some kind of regression analysis that tells you here's load times impact on MAOs.
turns.zh: 然后本质上有些回归分析会告诉你：加载时间对 MAO 的影响是这样的。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Exactly. And the other thing that we did is just so we would've these translation factors, but we could also just see what the cumulative impact of all of the work is that Facebook did this too, which is just long-term holdouts for each surface area. So the checkout experience team that I've been talking about a lot for some reason would have their own holdout. And so we could see what the cumulative impact of monthly active orders on the people that got last half's experience versus this half's experience on the holdout. And that would make it very clear. So regression is one way to do it. And then basically effective A/B test, but was a small holdout.
turns.zh: 没错。我们做的另一件事是，有了这些翻译系数，我们也能直接看所有工作的累计影响——Facebook 也这么干过，就是给每个界面区域留长期对照组。比如我一直在讲的结账体验团队，会有一个自己的对照组。所以我们能看到，拿到上半季体验的人和下半季体验的人，月活跃订单的累计影响差多少。这就非常清楚了。所以回归是一种方式。另一种基本上就是有效的 A/B 测试，只是用了一个小对照组。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a holdout for the performance team where someone just has a really slow version of Instacart?
turns.zh: 绩效团队也有对照组吗？就是有人拿到一个特别慢的 Instacart 版本？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: I wonder actually, but there's holdout for almost everything. There's a holdout for ads, for example. So there are some lucky Instacart users out there that are not getting ads and they've never gotten ads because they've always been part of Instacart's advertising holding.
turns.zh: 我其实也好奇，但几乎什么都留了对照组。比如广告就有对照组。所以有些幸运的 Instacart 用户从没看到过广告，因为他们一直都在 Instacart 的广告对照组里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That'll be a great revenue boost whenever they want to kill that holdout.
turns.zh: 等他们想关掉那个对照组，会是很大的收入提升。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Can you imagine was a conversation internally on should there be a permanent holdout? Should it be last year's experience? How should we think about, especially because it's such a important driver of modernization?
turns.zh: 你能想象这是个内部讨论：要不要永久对照组？应该是去年的体验吗？我们该怎么想，尤其因为它对现代化这么重要？
