turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe just one last question along this specific thread is this framework of having everything translated into a north star metric something you bring to every place you work now? And is this just something you recommend? For example, does Ramp approach things this way as well?
turns.zh: 顺着这条线最后一个问题：把一切都翻译到北极星指标这个框架，是你现在带到每个工作过的地方的吗？你只是推荐这个？比如 Ramp 也这么干吗？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: I think it depends on the size of the company. I think this actually becomes much more important as companies get bigger because there's more teams to prioritize and more resources to cross-allocate. And having a common currency makes that a lot easier. And so we do something similar at Ramp as well where we have translation factors for all of the various things that the teams are doing that translate back to the north star for Ramp.
turns.zh: 我觉得看公司规模。我觉得公司越大，这越重要，因为要排优先级的团队更多、要跨分配的资源更多。有一个通用货币让这事容易多了。所以我们在 Ramp 也做类似的事，给我们各种团队在做的东西建翻译系数，映射回 Ramp 的北极星。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. And then are you up for sharing the Ramp's north star metric or do you want to keep that part?
turns.zh: 酷。那你会愿意分享 Ramp 的北极星指标吗，还是想保留这块？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah, I mean I can tell you what we used to do in the recent past we're evolving some things and in the recent past it was for the growth team, the north star was dollars of SQL pipeline. So anything anybody did, we would try to estimate the impact into what would be the dollars of sales qualified lead pipeline generated for Ramp. So if the website team wanted to change language on the card's landing page, their direct impact would be conversion rate of email submission or something like that would be what they would be optimizing for. And then we would have, okay, what does two bips of conversion rate mean for dollars of SQL pipeline? A lot or not a lot? And depending on that, it's like, "All right, don't waste your time doing that project. Let's do something else instead." So that just helps us score and prioritize efforts.
turns.zh: 嗯，我可以告诉你我们最近过去是怎么做的，我们现在在演化一些东西。最近过去，对增长团队来说，北极星是「SQL 管道的美元数」。所以任何人做的任何事，我们都试着估算它对 Ramp 能产生多少销售合格线索管道的金额。比如网站团队想改卡片落地页的文案，他们的直接影响会是邮件提交的转化率之类的，那是他们要优化的。然后我们会算：转化率动两个基点，对 SQL 管道的美元数意味着多少？是大还是小？据此我们就说：「行了，别浪费时间做那个项目了，换个别的吧。」所以它帮我们打分、排优先级。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Here's a fun story. I actually tried to sign up for Ramp when I was starting this newsletter and business and it didn't let me because I had a Gmail-
turns.zh: 有个好玩的故事。我刚开始做这个通讯和生意时，其实试过注册 Ramp，但它没让我过，因为我用的是 Gmail——

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: For Gmail, yeah.
turns.zh: 对，Gmail 不行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I moved on and that would've been such a huge revenue opportunity. I'm just joking.
turns.zh: 所以我就走了，那本来会是个巨大的收入机会。我开玩笑的。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: I know, I know. And I'm glad you brought that up because we are obviously aware of it and we are working on something for users that have put in a personal email address. in terms of how to reengage that.
turns.zh: 我知道，我知道。而且我很高兴你提这个，因为我们显然知道这事，我们正针对那些填了个人邮箱的用户做点什么，关于怎么重新激活他们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're about to 5X growth because I had no other domain at that point. Now I have Lenny's newsletter and stuff, so it's like, "Shit, I'm stuck."
turns.zh: 你马上就要 5 倍增长了，因为那时候我没有任何别的域名。现在我有了 Lenny 的通讯之类的，所以就是「靠，我卡住了」。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: By the way, for anybody else that has that problem, they can just reach out to me, we'll figure it out. The reason we don't allow personal emails is because it's just typically very low in tech users that are coming to the website that are putting in personal emails.
turns.zh: 顺便，任何有这个问题的人，可以直接找我，我们搞定。我们不允许个人邮箱的原因，是来网站填个人邮箱的通常都是不太懂技术、不太对路的用户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Makes sense. I totally get it. I was not offended. I just like, all right. I had no way around it. That's the problem. So I like that you guys are adding some path around it and you're saying email you or reach out to you.
turns.zh: 有道理。我完全理解。我没生气。我就是，好吧，我没办法绕过去。问题就在这。所以我很高兴你们加了条路径，而且你说可以邮件你或者联系你。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: You can find me on Twitter or email me. I'm just as sribatchu@ramp.
turns.zh: 你可以在 Twitter 上找到我，或者邮件我，就是 sribatchu@ramp。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. You're going to have the most sales leads of any person at Ramp when this comes up. Okay. One other thing I wanted to touch on is success metrics. You talked about one of the keys to success and this repeatable growth engine is clear success metrics. Is there any just learnings and tips you have for people when they're thinking about success metrics?
turns.zh: 好。这期出来，你会是 Ramp 里拿到最多销售线索的人。好，另一件我想聊的是成功指标。你讲过，可重复增长引擎的关键之一是清晰的成功指标。当人们思考成功指标时，你有什么心得和贴士？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Finding the right success metric, there usually should be two. There should be one on volume and another one on efficiency. And we can talk about what are good efficiency metrics and what are good volume metrics. On volume, I think the right success metric has a couple things that are important. One is there's a clear linkage to value creation for the business. So if I move this metric that will drive revenue and which will drive equity value for the business or whatever it is that this particular. Metrics and for Facebook it was MAU, for Instacart, it was effectively monthly active orders, and it's something that we know is important that will really drive the value for the business, but it needs to have the other component of it, which is it's very intuitive for all of the people working internally to the company.
turns.zh: 找到对的成功指标，通常应该有两个。一个关于量，另一个关于效率。我们可以聊聊什么是好的效率指标、什么是好的量指标。关于量，我觉得对的成功指标有几个重要特征。一是它和业务创造价值之间有清晰的关联。所以如果我动这个指标，它会驱动营收，进而驱动业务的股权价值之类的。对每个业务，这指标不一样。对 Facebook 是 MAU，对 Instacart 实质上是月活跃订单，是我们都知道重要、会真正驱动业务价值的，但它还得有另一面：公司里所有内部的人都能很直觉地理解。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: And it's also clear, if they're working on some minutiae, how that can impact and actually move the main metric. So it's usually you have to find something that's somewhere in between, not too far, too lag, towards revenue and value creation, but also not something that's actually translatable to the efforts of various teams.
turns.zh: 而且要清楚，如果他们做的是某个细枝末节，那怎么能够真正拉动主指标。所以通常你要找一个中间的东西——不要太滞后、太偏向营收和价值创造，也不要离各团队的努力太远、无法翻译。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of a good success metric that just comes to mind to make this a little bit concrete for people?
turns.zh: 有没有一个具体的好成功指标例子，让这更接地气一点？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: It just depends on what goal at any given time is. Sometimes you're trying to drive more users, sometimes you're trying to drive more engagement and you can reorient the company on what you're trying to do as the north star for growth during that period of time. So users, obviously we've talked about as a good one. For engagement, I've often found what really helps is, and you've done actually really good benchmarking at some point, the escape velocity metric for growth for a company, I think.
turns.zh: 就看你某个时刻的目标是什么。有时你想驱动更多用户，有时想驱动更多参与度，你可以据此把公司重新定向到那个时期增长的北极星上。所以用户，显然我们聊过，是个好的。关于参与度，我常发现真正有用的是——你其实做过不错的基准——一个公司的「逃逸速度」指标。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: I don't think you phrased it that way, but that's [inaudible 00:45:18] for a given user, which is what does it take for somebody to become an engaged and active user or customer of a platform? And at Facebook, it was 10 friends the first seven days. At Instacart, it was three orders in the first month. And at Ramp, for our activation, I mean it's very specific to Ramp, but we've got four events that the customer needs to do in the first 30 days. And if they do that, they have a high likelihood of being activated and successful. So our activation team focuses on that.
turns.zh: 我猜你没这么叫，但那是指「对某个用户来说，要成为这个平台的活跃、参与用户需要什么」。在 Facebook，是头 7 天加 10 个朋友。在 Instacart，是头一个月下 3 单。在 Ramp，关于我们的激活，很具体，但我们有客户头 30 天要做的 4 个事件。如果他们做了，他们被激活、成功的概率就很高。所以我们的激活团队就专注这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The framework you just described reminds me Gibson Biddle has this really simple framework of gem where you can basically prioritize one of three things, growth, engagement, or monetization. And his advice is always just all of them are great, just make sure you're all aligned on which one matters most at the time.
turns.zh: 你刚描述的框架让我想起 Gibson Biddle 有个很简单的框架叫 GEM，你基本可以在增长、参与度、变现三者里挑一个优先。他的建议永远是：三个都好，只要确保你们对齐了当下哪个最重要。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah. And it is very similar to, we used to have this at Opendoor, and I think DoorDash also uses a similar framework, which is speed, quality, and cost. All three are important, but it's very hard to optimize all three at the same time. So you need to have a particular prioritization. And I think growth teams can also use that as, okay, I think the way I about the growth team's journey is step one is build a system that can move fast and then work on improving the quality and then work on optimization of cost after. So you pick which phase you're on because you can't do all three at the same time, whether it's growth, engagement, monetization, or just the other way of framing on it.
turns.zh: 对。而且这跟我们在 Opendoor 用的很像——我觉得 DoorDash 也用类似的——速度、质量、成本。三个都重要，但很难同时优化三个。所以你得有个特定的优先级。我觉得增长团队也可以这么用：我对增长团队的旅程是，第一步先建一个能快速行动的体系，然后提升质量，之后再优化成本。所以你要清楚自己处在哪个阶段，因为你不能三个同时做，无论是增长、参与度、变现，还是换个框架说。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of metrics, I have this note here that you're a big fan of payback period for measuring investment ROI versus CAC. Can you talk about why that is?
turns.zh: 说到指标，我这里有个笔记，说你特别推崇用「回收周期」而不是 CAC 来衡量投资 ROI。能讲讲为什么吗？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah. CAC obviously gets thrown around a lot and a lot of people are like, "Okay, you have to be reducing your CAC, CAC, CAC, CAC." There's a fundamental flaw to it which obviously is that you're focusing on cost and not the value derived. And so when you focus on CAC and reducing CAC, what tends to happen is you actually might be doing something very damaging where you're succeeding in reducing CAC, but you're actually bringing in customers that are less valuable because those are the ones that you're able to attract with a lower CAC. And so reframing it away from CAC towards LTV is helpful and that's better. So thinking about for better customers that are bigger, we want to spend more. So you might think, okay, well, LTV to CAC might be a better way of looking at that. I think the challenge with LTV to CAC especially for a lot of, even Ramp, it's only four years old, is it's really hard to predict LTV.
turns.zh: 对。CAC 显然被到处用，很多人说「你得降低你的 CAC、CAC、CAC」。它有个根本缺陷，就是它聚焦在成本而不是产生的价值。所以当你聚焦在 CAC、要降低 CAC 时，往往会发生很伤的事：你确实把 CAC 降下来了，但你招来的客户价值更低了，因为你能用低 CAC 吸引来的就是这类客户。所以把思路从 CAC 转向 LTV 是有帮助的，那更好。也就是对更大、更好的客户，我们愿意多花。你可能会想，那 LTV 对 CAC 也许是更好的视角。但我觉得 LTV 对 CAC 的挑战在于，哪怕对 Ramp——它才 4 岁——也很难预测 LTV。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: It's like a DCF, it's extremely assumption laden and it's hard to know what the final value will be. And especially if you think your churn is low and your LTV is very high, you might end up spending a lot of money because you're like, "Oh, my LTV to CAC is great." And then a year or two into the business, you realize actually your churn is higher than you thought. Your initial customers aren't representative of your long-term retention and all of a sudden you've destroyed a lot of value by looking at LTV to CAC, which is why I'm a big, big fan of payback period and actually being really thoughtful about that using contribution margin, not revenue or gross margin, like how long of contribution margin from this customer does it take to payback their cost? And setting this obviously is typically a mandate from the executive and board level on what is the payback period that we're comfortable with, and then just orienting everybody towards driving that blended payback period down as much as possible.
turns.zh: 它就像一个 DCF，极度依赖假设，你很难知道最终价值会是多少。尤其如果你觉得流失低、LTV 很高，你可能因为「哦我 LTV 对 CAC 很好」就花很多钱。然后业务过了一两年，你发现其实流失比你想的高，你最初的客户并不能代表长期留存，结果你因为看 LTV 对 CAC 毁掉了很多价值。这就是为什么我非常、非常推崇回收周期，并且真的要认真对待它——用贡献毛利，而不是营收或毛利率，也就是：从这个客户身上，要多少个月的贡献毛利才能收回获取他的成本？这显然通常由高管和董事会层面定下我们能接受的回收周期是多久，然后让所有人都朝把这个综合回收周期尽量压低的方向走。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For folks that aren't familiar with the concept of payback period or contribution margin, could you just briefly describe what those mean for listeners?
turns.zh: 对不熟悉回收周期或贡献毛利概念的人，你能简单描述一下它们是什么意思吗？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah, so contribution margin is basically the profit that you make on a given customer after you take into account all of the variable costs. So including the cost of production as well as any other variable costs to serve that customer. So that might include support and other things that scale with your revenue. And then payback period is literally just how many months of that profit would it take to pay for? Let's say it costs you $5,000 to acquire this customer and your estimated profit per month on the customer is 500. That is a 10-month payback period. So as I say that, I'm sure you've heard, you still have to make assumptions for payback period, but at least they're more based in recency and you can evaluate them more quickly.
turns.zh: 好，贡献毛利基本上就是你从某个客户身上赚的利润，扣掉所有可变成本。包括生产成本，以及任何随营收规模走的其他可变成本，比如支持和别的服务成本。然后回收周期字面意思就是：要多少个月的这种利润，才能覆盖获取成本？比如获取这个客户花了 5000 美元，估计这个客户每月利润是 500，那就是 10 个月的回收周期。我说这些的时候你也听出来了，回收周期你也得做假设，但至少它更贴近近期，你能更快地评估它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Thank you for doing that. Just a couple more questions around growth specifically. So there's a lot of ways to grow through the history of a company. You can invest in SEO, you can invest in paid and sales and referrals and influencer marketing, brand marketing, billboards, all these things. Do you have an opinion on how to sequence these sorts of bets for a company, especially in B2B?
turns.zh: 好，谢谢解释。关于增长再问几个问题。公司发展的历史上有很多增长方式。你可以投 SEO、付费、销售、推荐、 influencer 营销、品牌营销、广告牌，所有这些。你对一家公司怎么给这些押注排序有看法吗，尤其在 B2B？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Of course, a lot depends on who your customers are, what your unique value propositions are and how competitive the space that you're in. But I do think there's actually a general path that most B2B companies take and should take frankly, which is my view is you start off with founder-led sales, like the early team needs to know how to actually sell, then you hire your first couple of salespeople, then you start some very low cost targeted marketing efforts. So whether it's like content, community, small scale events, and then PR. After all of that is when you start paid and brand efforts. And then SEO probably start around the same time that you start paid marketing efforts.
turns.zh: 当然，很大程度取决于你的客户是谁、你的独特价值主张是什么、你所在领域竞争多激烈。但我确实觉得，大多数 B2B 公司实际走的、而且理应走的，有一条相对固定的路径——我的看法是先从创始人主导的销售开始，早期团队得真的会卖；然后招头几个销售；然后开始一些成本很低、很精准的营销动作，比如内容、社群、小规模活动，再然后是 PR。所有这些之后，才开始的付费和品牌投入。SEO 大概和你开始做付费营销同时启动。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: The reason for the progression the way I've described it is the channels get more expensive as you go farther along and they get more effective as you understand more about your customers and they're more scalable as well as you go farther along the list that I've described. And so that's the intention behind sequencing in that way. SEO is a bit unique. The reason I recommend it later rather than earlier, even though it's not necessarily that expensive, is just take some time to build. And without domain authority or backlinking or any media presence, you can end up just flailing with SEO, creating content and not getting any actual traction for a long time. So there's usually a good inflection point for your company to double down on SEO efforts. And it's somewhat a little bit later than some of the other times.
turns.zh: 我这么排顺序的原因是：越往后的渠道越贵，但你越了解客户，它们也越有效、也越能规模化。这就是这么排的意图。SEO 有点特殊。我建议它靠后而不是靠前，尽管它不一定贵，是因为它需要时间积累。没有域名权重、没有反向链接、没有任何媒体存在感，你做 SEO 可能只是在那扑腾——一直产内容却长期没 traction。所以公司通常有个好的拐点，才该在 SEO 上加倍投入，而这个点比别的一些动作要晚一些。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This touches on a great line that you have around experimentation where you talk about how you don't want to just fail fast with an experiment. You want to fail conclusively, if that's the word. Is that right? And then can you talk about that?
turns.zh: 这关联到你关于实验的一句很棒的话：你说你不想只是「快速失败」，你想「彻底地失败」，如果这是那个词的话？对吗？能聊聊这个吗？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah, I talk a lot about that with my teams both here and other places, which is we celebrate failure. Growth experiments in my history are typically 30%-ish success rate. So the vast majority of things that you try don't work. And so you want to create a culture where people aren't afraid to take risks and aren't afraid to fail. And for me, failure is not that you didn't drive revenue, failure is not learning. So it's really important that you learn when you fail. And so we celebrate failure as long as you're learning and you can only learn if you've designed the right test and you failed conclusively because otherwise, I think many of us have been in situations where there's intuition that something might work and it doesn't work, and then you end up doing it over and over for years because every time a new executive or somebody else has the same idea, you try it again and it's because you haven't been able to design the test to fail conclusively, and it's hard to do.
turns.zh: 对，我和我的团队在这儿和别的地方都常聊这个：我们庆祝失败。我历史上增长实验的成功率大概只有 30% 左右。所以你试的绝大多数东西都不行。所以你要营造一种文化，让人不害怕冒险、不害怕失败。而对我来说，失败不是「你没带来营收」，失败是「没学到东西」。所以你失败时能学到东西才重要。我们庆祝失败，前提是你学到了——而你只有设计了正确的测试、并且「彻底地失败」了，才能学到，因为否则的话，我想很多人都有过这种处境：直觉觉得某东西可能行，结果不行，然后你年复一年地一遍遍试，因为每次新高管或别人有同样想法，你又试一次——就是因为你没能把测试设计到能「彻底失败」，而那很难。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: But at the end of the day, there's only two ways to make an experiment successful. Either you have a very large M or have a very significant treatment, which is what you're doing in the experiment itself. And in B2B, you don't usually have the luxury of large M, which you do in consumer. Facebook can get stats taken in two hours. A B2B company could take two years to get the same number of touch points. And so to counteract that, I recommend people just trying to maximize the treatment effect, which is if you have a hypothesis that you're testing, just throw all of the possible tactics and resources that you think would move that needle because you can always cost rationalize later if it works.
turns.zh: 但说到底，让一个实验成功只有两种方式。要么你有非常大的 M（样本量），要么你有非常大的处理效应（treatment）——也就是你在实验本身里做的改变。在 B2B，你通常没有大 M 的奢侈，那是消费端才有的。Facebook 两小时就能拿到统计结果。一家 B2B 公司可能要两年才能拿到同样多的触点。所以为了对抗这个，我建议大家尽量最大化处理效应——如果你有个在测的假设，就把所有你觉得能撬动那个指针的战术和资源都砸上去，因为成了你总能事后算账、合理化成本。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: And so just maximize the treatment effect. And if with all of that it didn't work, then you can say, "Hey, we're not going to try this again because we literally did try everything that we could to test this hypothesis." And if it doesn't work in the best version and it's expensive as it is, this is not worth spending more time on. But if it does work, great, then you do another version of the test with half the tactics or whichever tactics you think work better or worse and you optimize over time.
turns.zh: 所以就最大化处理效应。如果那样都还不行，那你就能说：「嘿，我们不会再试这个了，因为我们真的是把所有能试的都试了来验证这个假设。」如果它在最好的版本里都不行、又这么贵，那就不值得再花时间。但如果它行，太好了，那你再做一个版本，去掉一半战术，或者你觉得更好或更差的那些，随着时间优化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example you could share when you did that?
turns.zh: 你能分享一个你这么做的例子吗？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: I mean, account based marketing is something that is very common in enterprise software where you've selected certain customers that you think are high priority and you're saying, "I want to touch them in as many nuanced ways possible to see if that drives conversion." And this is something I've seen tried many times where people do it, but they do it halfway where they're like, "Okay, tried these three things. Conversion of the control group wasn't higher. And so we think this is not going to work."
turns.zh: 嗯，基于客户的营销（ABM）在企业软件里很常见：你选了一些你觉得高优先级的客户，说「我想用尽可能多、尽可能细腻的方式去触达他们，看能不能拉动转化」。这东西我看过很多人试，但他们试一半就放弃了，说「好了，试了这三招。对照组转化没更高，所以我们觉得这不行」。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: And then a new go-to market executive comes and they have to do it again. They have to do it again. They have to do it again. It's a very common one wherever this happens. And so when we did it at Ramp, we did exactly what I just described, which is let's really be thoughtful about the experiment design, both in terms of maximizing the number of people as well as maximizing the number of ways and types of ways that we're effectively touching these target customers to show the value one way or the other.
turns.zh: 然后一个新来的市场进入（go-to-market）高管来了，又得再做一次、再做一次、再做一次。这事儿在哪儿都很常见。所以我们在 Ramp 做的时候，就是严格按我刚说的来：让我们真的在实验设计上很讲究，既最大化触达的人数，也最大化我们触达这些目标客户的方式和类型的数量，好让价值以这样或那样的方式显现出来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what it sounds like is the hypothesis isn't like this email will have a big impact on conversion. It's like this strategy of coming after customers is what we're testing.
turns.zh: 所以听起来，假设不是「这封邮件会对转化有很大影响」，而是「我们测的是这种追客户的方式」。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: That's the example there. And I think for example, this kind of framework is more important for cross-functional, larger scale, bigger tests rather than an email modification. But we could even use it on a micro example, like an email modification where you are like, okay, I think this particular email is underperforming because it's not talking to this part of the customer's pain point or journey or what have you. And the simplest test would be, okay, let me make some tweaks to the text and edit that, and that could be the end of that test.
turns.zh: 那是那个例子。我觉得这种框架对跨职能、更大规模、更大的测试更重要，而不是对一个邮件的小修改。但我们也能用在微观例子上，比如邮件修改：你觉得这封特定的邮件表现不好，因为它没讲到客户痛点或旅程的某个部分。最简单的测试就是：好，我改改文案、编辑一下，测试就结束了。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: And if that doesn't work, you're like, "Oh, maybe those weren't the right text edits. Let me do a different text edits or whatever." And that's fine, that's low cost. It's not the end of the world for you to be wrong there. But an alternative that you could do is like, oh, what are all of the things that I could change about this email in the same test? Is it the trigger of the email? Is it the text content of the email? Is it additional personalization? Is it the design of the email? Trying to think of what are all of the various levers that you think could be wrong and put them all together to test your hypothesis of this touchpoint is wrong and how do I improve that.
turns.zh: 如果那不行，你会想「哦，可能那些文案改得不对，我换个文案改法」。那也行，成本低，你错了也没什么大不了。但另一种做法是：哦，关于这封邮件，我在同一个测试里能改的所有东西是什么？是触发时机？是邮件文案内容？是额外的个性化？是邮件设计？去想所有你觉得可能出错的杠杆，把它们全放一起，来测你的假设——这个触点有问题，我怎么改进它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, obviously the downside of that is if it doesn't work, you don't know if it's like, oh, maybe it was this thing could have worked in the subject-
turns.zh: 不过显然这种做法是，如果它不行，你不知道是不是「哦，可能就是主题行那个能行」——

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah. So there's always trade-offs on this. But what you're hoping is you've done a complete refresh where you did all the things that you thought were intuitive that should work. And if it doesn't work, then you're like, "Okay, maybe my hypothesis is wrong." But you're right. There's always going to be a challenge if maybe the execution is wrong and I did too many things potentially in that case.
turns.zh: 对。所以这里永远有取舍。但你希望的是，你做了一次彻底的刷新，把所有你觉得直觉上应该行的都做了。如果不行，那你就像「好吧，可能我的假设是错的」。但你说得对，总会有这种挑战：也许执行错了，而我那次可能放太多东西进去了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How does that go with the velocity culture? Is it just do those things real fast even though it's not like micro optimize, it's like go bigger but do them fast?
turns.zh: 这和速度文化怎么协调？就是那些事也做得很快，即使不是微优化，而是更大但做得快？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. So that's why I think it's important to frame where this matters. And so I think I'm less worried about failing conclusively for things that you can fail really, really fast and just redo, right? Things like website conversion, email, et cetera. I'm more worried about that for things that take a while to plan and cost money, et cetera.
turns.zh: 对，对。所以这就是为什么我觉得讲清楚这适用于哪儿很重要。对于那些你能极快失败、然后重来的东西——比如网站转化、邮件之类的——我不太担心要彻底失败。我更担心的是那些要花时间规划、又要花钱的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Okay. Great. Maybe one last question around growth specifically. What are some of your favorite tools for the growth team, either internally, whatever you can share, or externally that just allow you to operate efficiently and effectively?
turns.zh: 懂了。好，很棒。关于增长最后一个问题。你最喜欢增长团队用的哪些工具，无论是内部的、你能分享的，还是外部的，能让你高效运作的？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: A couple of things that we've used, I mean, one simple thing is for sprint planning, actually, we use Airtable because the planning process and the scoring is so much more analytical and the translation layer. So we've got a template on how we do our sprint planning and how we translate the various impact metrics into the common currency, which I enjoy, but I don't see it has to be Airtable. It's just some form of organization that works well for that. In terms of a very tactical growth tool that we've enjoyed recently is we used this company called Mutiny, which is also around customer, which is a tool for website copy, personalization. So they hook up with our third party data sources that we pay for, and based on what we know about the customer as they're landing on our page, we can personalize, copy, and design based on that. And that's had material impact and allowed us to scale website experimentation.
turns.zh: 我们用的几样东西，一个简单的是冲刺规划，其实我们用 Airtable，因为规划流程和打分非常分析化，还有那个翻译层。我们有个模板，讲怎么跑冲刺规划、怎么把各种影响指标翻译成通用货币，我很喜欢，但我也不觉得非得是 Airtable，只要是某种好用的组织方式就行。说到最近我们很喜欢的非常战术性的增长工具，我们用了一家叫 Mutiny 的公司，也是跟客户相关的，是个做网站文案个性化的工具。它接上我们付费买的第三方数据源，基于我们对登录页面的客户的了解，我们能据此个性化文案和设计。这带来了实质影响，还让我们能规模化地做网站实验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And then are there internal tools you've built to help with experimentation or I don't know, sharing data, dashboard? I don't know, is there anything else that's just like, wow, this really helps us move fast?
turns.zh: 太棒了。那有没有你们内部搭建的、用来帮实验或者分享数据、仪表盘的工具？还有什么让你觉得「哇，这真的帮我们跑得快」的？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Eric, our CEO, has publicly talked about this. I think we as a company are very thoughtful about what we build in-house versus what we buy externally. I think a lot of engineering teams are often excited about building things in-house where there's off the shelf products that could basically work externally. And Ramp has historically been good at not falling into that trap. And we use third party tools for a lot of our growth and experimentation for things that are not proprietary, strategic, et cetera, obviously. Some of the automation stuff that we've talked about, we've built all of that in-house in terms of prospecting, lead scoring, and how we talk to our customers. But for the most part, we use external tools. Instacart and Opendoor were not like that. We built our own internal experiment tracking systems, A/B testing frameworks and all of that in-house.
turns.zh: 我们的 CEO Eric 公开聊过这个。我觉得我们作为一家公司，对什么自己搭、什么外部买，非常讲究。很多工程团队常常对自建很兴奋，但其实有现成的产品外部基本就能用。Ramp 历史上一直比较能避免掉进这个坑。对非专有、非战略性的东西，我们大量用第三方工具来做增长和实验。当然，我们聊过的一些自动化——潜在客户开发、线索打分、以及我们怎么跟客户沟通——这些是我们全部自建的。但绝大多数我们用外部工具。Instacart 和 Opendoor 不是这样，我们自建了内部的实验追踪系统、A/B 测试框架，全都自己搭。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's what I would've guessed about Ramp that it's with speed, you got to not build stuff you don't have to build. So that makes a lot of sense. Okay. Maybe one last topic to talk about. I want to talk about hiring. You have some really interesting approaches to how to think about hiring. One is I think you have a really interesting strategy for how to find the best companies and also the best people at each of those companies to go after if you're hiring for specific role. Can you talk about how you think about that?
turns.zh: 这倒是我就猜到的 Ramp 的样子——讲速度嘛，你就不该建那些没必要建的东西。很有道理。好，最后一个话题。我想聊聊招聘。你对怎么思考招聘有一些特别有意思的思路。其中一个是，我觉得你有个很有意思的策略，关于如果你要为某个特定角色招人，怎么找到最好的公司、以及每家公司里最好的人去追。能讲讲你是怎么想的吗？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Gokul on Twitter has talked about some of those, which is there's two ways to go about hiring great people. One way is basically a very thoughtful and tactical network search where let's say you're hiring for a head of SEO, you go ask your network of who is the best SEO person you know, get introduction to each of those folks, and then ask them who the best person that they know is. And you have a mapping of where are the best SEO teams and why. If you can't get one of those people, 20, 30 people on your target list, you go down the list of, okay, what is the next best person? And you typically want to limit it to companies that are one to two stages of growth after you. So you want somebody that has seen your stage of growth and beyond at a company that has a reputation for craft and the field that you're looking for. So that's a very classic way of doing that, and I think that works really well for people and companies that are really well-connected.
turns.zh: Gokul 在 Twitter 上聊过一些，就是招牛人有两种方式。一种是非常讲究、战术性的「人脉搜索」：比如你要招一个 SEO 负责人，你去问你的人脉「你认识的最好的 SEO 是谁」，去认识那些人，再问他们「你认识的最好的 SEO 是谁」。你就有了「最好的 SEO 团队都在哪、为什么」的地图。如果你目标名单上那 20、30 个人一个都拿不下，你就往下走：「好，下一个最好的人是谁？」通常你想把范围限制在你之后一到两个增长阶段的公司。也就是你要找见过你这个增长阶段、甚至更多阶段的人，而且那家公司在你要找的那个领域以工艺（craft）著称。这是很经典的方式，我觉得对那些人脉很广的人和公司特别好用。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: So there's another approach that I've actually used successfully is much more kind of data driven and external and not as network based, which is you can often look up data. [inaudible 01:02:14] is a lot of it is somewhat public, right? So you can look up information on which companies might be doing well. So for example, I'll just pick like if you're looking for great email marketing folks like CRM marketing lead or something like that, you can actually look up on similar web, what percentage of traffic shows up via email to companies websites. So you've got your target list of companies that are one or two stage beyond you that you respect as general companies. And you can go and see, okay, which ones of these are actually really effective at driving web traffic or app traffic or app downloads via their email. And then go try to source from those teams and companies. And I think people under-utilize that even though it's very intuitive, it's just not something that occurs to people to do.
turns.zh: 我其实成功用过另一种更数据驱动、更外部、不那么靠人脉的方式：你常常能查到数据。[听不清] 很多东西其实某种程度上是公开的，对吧？所以你能查到哪些公司可能表现好。比如我就随便举，如果你在找很厉害的邮件营销的人——比如 CRM 营销负责人之类的——你其实能在 SimilarWeb 上查到，有多少流量是通过邮件到公司网站的。所以你有一份你尊重的、比你领先一到两个阶段的目标公司名单，然后你去看看，这些里哪些真的能很有效地通过邮件驱动网站或 App 流量、或 App 下载。然后去那些团队和公司里挖人。我觉得这个被低估了，虽然它很直觉，就是大家不会想到去做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I've not heard that tip right there. The first piece, Google definitely recommends this, and I think the core part of that is the core theme here is find the companies that are the best at the thing you're trying to hire for, and then figure out who at the company is the best once you start talking to people. I love it. Another strong opinion that I think you have is around paying people and how much to pay the best. Can you talk about that?
turns.zh: 我喜欢。我之前没听过这个贴士。第一点，Google 肯定推荐这个，我觉得核心主题是：找到在你要招的那件事上最强的公司，然后开始跟人聊的时候，搞清楚那家公司里谁最强。我喜欢。你另一个很强的观点，是关于怎么付钱、给最好的人付多少。能聊聊吗？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah, I think there's a lot of conversation around compensation is very much focused on equality and narrowing the gap and bands for compensation. And I think personally, I know it's a bit of a spicy take maybe, but I think it's the exact opposite direction of the conversation that companies should be having about compensation, which is I strongly, strongly believe that small teams of successful people can drive a lot more impact than larger teams of mediocre people.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得关于薪酬有太多讨论聚焦在平等、缩小差距和薪酬带宽上。我个人觉得——我知道这可能有点辣——但我觉得公司该聊薪酬的方向，正好相反：我强烈、强烈相信，一小群成功的人能比一大群平庸的人带来大得多的产出。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: And so I strongly believe you have to design a system where you're able to reward 10X operators with 10X the comp. You certainly see that at the executive level. So if you look at the same executive at different companies at similar stages, the comp can be widely different based for a variety of reasons. But one of them is the perception of performance and potential by the management team. And I think people need to be thinking about how to do that across more levels, which is if you can do that, and if you do that well, I think you're able to differentially hire and retain the best talent. And that'll be a great competitive advantage for companies that can do that well.
turns.zh: 所以我相信你必须设计一套系统，让你能用 10 倍的薪酬奖励 10 倍的操盘手。你在高管层当然看得到这个。同样的高管，在不同类似阶段的公司，薪酬可能因为各种原因差很多。其中一个原因是管理层对其表现和潜力的判断。我觉得大家要想的是怎么在更多层级上这么做——如果你能做到、而且做得好，你就能差异化地招到并留住最好的人才。这对能做到的公司会是巨大的竞争优势。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And do you think about this within a team pay the best people the most, or is it more only hire these 10X people and then pay everyone the most?
turns.zh: 你是想在团队内部「给最好的人最多钱」，还是说更偏向于「只招这些 10 倍人才、然后给所有人最高薪酬」？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: People think of the talent density of your company as dependent on hiring. And that's obviously true. It's an important part of the ecosystem and the first part, but it's equally dependent on retention and performance management. A lot of companies can be good at hiring, but hiring has pretty high rate of false positive. Interview is the worst, best way to hire somebody. And then there's lots of ways you can make the interviewing process better, make it more interactive, make it more effective, but at the end of the day, you still don't know about someone until you really work closely with the new team, with the new mandate at your company.
turns.zh: 大家把公司的人才密度想成只取决于招聘。那当然对，是生态系统重要的一部分、也是第一步，但它同样取决于留存和绩效管理。很多公司擅长招人，但招聘的误招率相当高。面试是招人最糟、却也是最好的方式。然后有很多方法能让面试流程更好、更互动、更有效，但说到底，在新人真正和你团队紧密共事、接手新任务之前，你还是不了解他。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: So I think it's not about necessarily hiring [inaudible 01:05:44] operators, obviously you're looking for that, but it's also about investing in people that are doing really well and accelerating their growth and rewards based on impact once they're there and as well as managing out people directly that didn't work out. And I typically think it's almost never when I've had to part ways with people is because someone's a bad actor. It's almost always that it just wasn't the right fit for whatever reason, for their skillset, for their life goals or whatever it may be. And it just wasn't a fit for that role. And I think a lot of companies are hesitant to make those changes, and I think that's how they bring their talent bar down, frankly.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得，重点不一定是非要招[听不清]操盘手，你当然在找那种人，但同样重要的是投资那些表现很好的人，基于他们来了之后的影响加速他们的成长和奖励，以及直接管理掉那些不合适的人。我不得不让人离开时，几乎从来不是因为谁是个坏人，几乎总是因为不管出于什么原因——技能、人生目标什么的——就是不合适。而很多公司犹豫做这些改变，我觉得那正是他们把人才门槛拉低的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely agree. Sri, is there anything else that you wanted to touch on before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 完全同意。Sri，在进入超刺激的快问快答之前，还有什么你想聊的吗？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: I don't know how many people will use this. I'm still surprised when new folks come to me and it's like I need to write, by the way, a document of how do you work with me? Because I know it's a lot of people have been talking about, I think [inaudible 01:06:51] Johnson's talked about it too, but I say that my love languages are spreadsheets and frameworks. And one very simple one that I've always liked that sometimes people surprised to hear, but it's most consultants know is what we call MECE, mutually exclusive, collectively exhausted set of things. So whenever you're trying to attack a problem and trying to brainstorm solutions or what have you, I really like to remind the teams to think about MECE because when you think about that and evaluate your set of solutions with that framework in mind, I think you tend to find that you've catch more potential solutions and also you'll feel comfortable that you've been comprehensive in your solution development. So anyway, just a little thing for people that are earlier in their careers to not forget.
turns.zh: 我不知道多少人会用这个。新同事来找我时我还是会惊讶，就像我得写一份「怎么跟我共事」的文档。我知道很多人在聊这个，我觉得[听不清] Johnson 也聊过，但我说我的「爱的语言」是电子表格和框架。有个我很喜欢、有时大家听了会意外的简单框架，但多数顾问都知道，叫 MECE——相互独立、完全穷尽的一组东西。所以每当你要攻一个问题、头脑风暴解决方案时，我很喜欢提醒团队用 MECE 来想，因为用这个框架去评估你那组解决方案时，你往往会发现能兜住更多潜在的方案，也会对你已经做得很全面感到安心。总之，给职业生涯早期的人一个小提醒，别忘了这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's make it a little bigger than a little thing. So MECE, mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive. Is there an example of what that may look like and or visualize for people to think about what this means in practice?
turns.zh: 那我们让这个小提醒变得大一点。MECE，相互独立、完全穷尽。能不能给个例子，或者让人想象一下这在实践里长什么样？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, I'll give it really dumb example, but that will make the point hopefully. It's like, okay, our profitability or our revenue growth has slowed down is the problem that you're trying to solve. And so okay, you start with, okay, what does this mean? You've got revenue per user has gone down, or customer has gone down, or number of customers have slowed down. Okay, that's step one of the MECE framework. Then it's like, okay, where does the revenue come from? What are all the various products that revenue could be coming from? Has it changed on any one of them? And then customers, why have customers gone down? Is it new customer acquisition? Is it activation of customers that have signed up? Is it retention? And just breaking that problem. So at each layer you've collectively exhausted all of the possible ways that this problem could have arrived. And just having that framework whenever you approach every problem will prevent you from missing something important. And also just more generally give you an others' confidence that you're being comprehensive in your solution development.
turns.zh: 好，我给个很傻但 hopefully 能说明问题的例子。比如「我们的盈利或收入增长放缓了」是你要解决的问题。好，你开始拆：这是什么意思？是每用户收入降了，还是客户数降了，还是客户数增速慢了？好，这是 MECE 框架第一步。然后：收入从哪来？所有可能出收入的产品的收入都来自哪？其中哪个变了？然后客户这块，为什么客户数降了？是新客获取？是注册用户的激活？是留存？就这样把问题拆开。所以每一层，你都完全穷尽了这个问题可能出现的所有方式。每次你用这个框架去攻任何问题，它都会防止你漏掉重要的东西，也总体上给别人一种信心：你的方案是全面的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So one way to think about this in this specific case is just make a formula of all of the variables that play into the question you're trying to answer.
turns.zh: 懂了。所以在这个具体例子里，一种理解方式是：就把所有影响你想回答的那个问题的变量列成一个公式。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Well, Sri, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好。Sri，说到这儿，我们到了超刺激的快问快答环节。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah, let's do it.
turns.zh: 准备好了，来吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 你最常推荐给别人的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: I tend to find most business books can be decks, but one that I really like actually is Never Split The Difference by Chris Voss. It's a negotiation book, find it super helpful for negotiation, but also for a lot of business decision making generally, to be honest, and life. And then I'm a big fan of sci-fi short stories, so anything by Ted Chiang or Ken Liu, I highly recommend.
turns.zh: 我发现大多数商业书其实都能做成几页 deck，但有一本我真的很喜欢，是 Chris Voss 的《Never Split The Difference》（绝不妥协）。是本谈判书，我觉得它对谈判、对一般商业决策、甚至对生活都超级有用。然后我很喜欢科幻短篇，所以 Ted Chiang 或 Ken Liu 的任何作品，我强烈推荐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love those both. On the first one I'm actually in the process of listening to it on audio and every time I'm in a place where I can negotiate something, I never remember anything that I've learned. Is there one thing that you've taken away from that book that stuck with you of like I use this?
turns.zh: 这两本我都喜欢。第一本我其实正在听有声书，但每次到一个能谈判的场合，我什么都想不起来。书里有没有哪一点你一直记着、真的在用的？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: I think that the core of the book really is about listening behind the problem of negotiation and what is the person really asking for. So his example of if you're always trying to split things evenly, you'll end up with one brown shoe, one black shoe, where neither of you are happy. And so rather than thinking about BATNA and ZOPA and all the other business school frameworks on negotiation, I think focus on deep down what does this other person want and how can I change the conversation about that rather than the thing that we're arguing over.
turns.zh: 我觉得这本书的核心，是关于在谈判的问题背后去听：这个人真正要的是什么。他举的例子是，如果你总想平分，你会落得一只有棕鞋、一只黑鞋，谁都不开心。所以与其想 BATNA、ZOPA 那些商学院框架，我觉得要聚焦在：这个人深层的欲望是什么，我怎么把对话从我们在争的东西，转到那个欲望上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Great. Next question. What's a favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 好。下一个问题。最近喜欢的电影或剧集？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: I mean, obviously it won the Oscar, but I really enjoyed Everything Everywhere All at Once. I thought it was such a wonderful story and really I think it's one of those... It's funny. The movie can also be, I think, everything because there are just so many different reads that you can get about that. It's about family, it's about immigration, it's about love. There's a lot of really interesting themes explored via one movie.
turns.zh: 显然它拿了奥斯卡，但我真的很喜欢《瞬息全宇宙》（Everything Everywhere All at Once）。我觉得故事特别好，而且它属于那种……很有意思，这部电影也可以是「一切」，因为你能从里面读出太多不同的东西。它关于家庭、关于移民、关于爱。一部电影里探索了很多很有意思的主题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's a favorite interview question you like to ask?
turns.zh: 你喜欢问的面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: I was going to say, oh, I like to ask other people.
turns.zh: 我刚想说，哦，我喜欢问别人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You like to ask. What did you think I was going to ask?
turns.zh: 你喜欢问。你以为我要问什么？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Oh, I thought what was my favorite interview question that you've asked or others have asked?
turns.zh: 哦，我以为是「你最喜欢、或者别人问过的最喜欢的面试问题是什么？」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, I got to clarify this. Both are acceptable answers.
turns.zh: 哦，我得澄清一下。两个答案都接受。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: I was going to cheat on that one and say the one that you asked me right before, because I'm a big fan of actually movies and TV shows and people rarely ask about that interviews like this, but favorite interview that I'd like to ask candidates actually is what's something that you're really bad at but you still do and why?
turns.zh: 我本来想在那题上耍赖，说你刚问我的那个，因为我超爱电影和剧集，这种面试很少问，但我真正喜欢问候选人的问题是：有什么事你其实很糟、却还在做，为什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you look for in their answer when you ask them?
turns.zh: 你从他们的回答里看什么？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah, a lot of people actually struggle with that question and can't answer anything that they do that they're bad at, which is a little bit of a yellow flag, which means that they're only used to doing things that they're successful at and they haven't cultivated interests that are not correlated to their own success at doing something. And they haven't taken the time to do that. And folks like that are going to run at the first sign of trouble and be like, "Oh, I'm not successful at this, so I'm going to move on." And what I really want to see is people that show examples of things that they're not successful at that they do for other motivations and goals and interests. And so if you can tell me a compelling story like that, it's usually a winning answer so to speak.
turns.zh: 对，很多人其实答不上来，说不出自己有什么做得糟的事，这有点是个黄旗——说明他们只习惯做自己成功的事，没培养起和「自己成功」不相关的兴趣。他们没花时间去那样做。这类人一遇到麻烦就会跑，说「哦我不成功，所以我走」。我真正想看到的是，有人能举出例子：他们不成功、却出于别的动机、目标或兴趣还在做的事。所以如果你能给我讲一个这样有说服力的故事，通常就是个「赢」的答案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite product or two that you've recently discovered that you love?
turns.zh: 你最近发现、很喜欢的一两个产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Carrie mentioned Eight Sleep once in this call. I love my Eight Sleep. I'm a big fan and they're Ramp customers as well. And so that's been a great pandemic purchase. So I guess maybe not as recent. And then maybe another one is Fellow coffee, their kettles I think just designed so beautifully. I don't drink coffee, I drink tea, but I use my Fellow kettle for tea, and I think it's just a delightful product to use.
turns.zh: Carrie 这通电话里提过一次 Eight Sleep。我很爱我的 Eight Sleep。我是大粉丝，他们也是 Ramp 的客户。所以那是很好的疫情期购买。可能不算最近。另一个可能是 Fellow 的咖啡具，他们的水壶设计得真美。我不喝咖啡，喝茶，但用 Fellow 的水壶烧茶，我觉得用起来就是个让人愉悦的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I got a Fellow kettle from my tea also, and I found that the flow of the water was too slow and it's just standing here pouring this pour over.
turns.zh: 我也有个 Fellow 水壶，用来烧茶，但我发现出水太慢了，就在这儿站着倒这个手冲。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. So they do have a non-pour over kettle, which is what I have, which makes it easier.
turns.zh: 对，对。他们有不是手冲款的水壶，我用的就是那个，更好用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. My mistake. Next question. What is something relatively minor you've changed in your product development process that you found to have a big impact on your ability to execute?
turns.zh: 好，我的错。下一个问题。在你的产品开发流程里，你改过什么相对小的东西，却对执行能力有很大的影响？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, I don't know if this is minor or not, but one of the things that on the growth side, we used to have separate sprint planning for the product team, for the marketing teams, and each team had their own planning cycles. And one of the things that we did is we brought them all together into one. So the lifecycle marketers joined the product activation team sprint cycles, and so their projects and work are very tightly aligned and work in the same pace and system as the rest of the product team. And that's had tremendous impact in our ability to work together.
turns.zh: 嗯，我不知道这算不算小，但增长这边有一件事：我们以前产品团队、营销团队各自有单独的冲刺规划，每个团队有自己的规划周期。我们做的一件事是把它们合到一起。所以生命周期营销的人加入了产品激活团队的冲刺周期，于是他们的项目和工作和产品团队其他人是同一个节奏、同一个系统在跑。这对我们一起协作的能力影响巨大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question, Ramp is all about helping people save money. I'm curious if you have any tips on just saving money.
turns.zh: 最后一个问题，Ramp 就是帮人省钱的。我好奇你有没有什么省钱的小贴士。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: I mean, it seems obvious, and I think I feel like negotiation's already been the theme of this lightning round, but everything is negotiable when it comes to contracts. People think contracts are standardized for software and usually not. People are trying to sell you something they're trying to grow too. They have their quotas to meet, they have their goals to hit. So I mean, Ramp obviously has a service for this if you wanted to scale these Ramps, but you can do this on your own. Always try to negotiate, be mindful of quarter ends for salespeople. And so if you can push something out till near the end of the quarter, you can ask for, "Hey, I'll sign it by the end of the month if you give me a 10% discount," will often work. So there's tips like that you can do, but remember that you can always negotiate.
turns.zh: 嗯，这好像很明显，而且我觉得谈判已经是这轮快问快答的主题了，但合同里一切皆可谈。大家觉得软件的合同是标准化的，通常并不是。人家也想把东西卖给你、自己也要增长。他们有配额要完成、有目标要达成。所以如果要用 Ramp 来规模化做这些，Ramp 显然有这个服务，但你自己也能做。永远试着去谈，留意销售人员的季度末。所以如果你能把一件事推到季度末附近，你可以说「我月底签，你给我 9 折」，通常能成。所以有这类贴士，但记住：你永远能谈。

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: And then the second one is, I would say is just hire slower. I'm a big believer in, and Geoff talks about this too in your other interview, hiring based on slope rather than intercept, I think will work well for you and only hiring when people and teams are really stretched. I think this will serve you well both on cost and on impact. There'll be plenty of scope for the people that you hire, and as I said, I'm a big believer in small teams accomplishing more like Ramp being like a fraction of the size of some of our competitors with similar orders of revenue.
turns.zh: 第二点是，我会说招人慢一点。我深信，而且 Geoff 在你另一次采访里也聊过，按「斜率」而不是「截距」来招人，对你会有用，而且只在人或团队真的被压得不行时才招。我觉得这点在成本和产出上都会对你很好。你招来的人会有大把施展空间，而且就像我说过，我深信小团队能完成更多——就像 Ramp 体量只有某些竞争对手的一小部分，收入却是一个量级。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sure. We've covered velocity, growth, hiring. So many topics, everything I was hoping we touch on. Two final questions, where can folks find you if they want to reach out and learn more and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 当然。我们聊了速度、增长、招聘。这么多话题，都是我希望聊到的。最后两个问题：大家想联系你、多了解，去哪找你？听众能怎么帮到你？

turns.speaker: Sri Batchu
turns.en: Yeah, I'm a big fan of the fun place of the cesspool of Twitter, so I have a public Twitter account that you can DM me. My DMs are open, it's just my name's sri_batchu. And in terms of listeners can be useful, honestly, I think I really enjoy meeting like-minded folks, and as I may have mentioned in other places, Ramp is growing incredibly well and we're constantly looking to hire and we're still hiring. So if you know best in class growth in marketing folks that they can recommend that we hire at Ramp, I'd love to hear.
turns.zh: 对，我是那个有趣的地方、Twitter 这个粪坑的粉丝，所以我有公开 Twitter 账号，可以私信我。我的私信是开的，就是我名字 sri_batchu。至于听众能帮上什么，说实话，我真的很喜欢认识志同道合的人，而且就像我别处提过的，Ramp 增长得极好，我们一直在招人、现在还在招。所以如果你认识顶尖的增长或营销人才，能推荐来 Ramp 招的，我很想听。
